9.8 — The Internet: Packets, Routing & DNS

Every git push this semester split your work into packets, addressed them, and let strangers' machines forward them across the planet. Today: what actually happens in those two seconds — the exam's CSN-1 family, told through the command you have typed a hundred times.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Packets, not streams. Nothing crosses the internet whole. Your 2 MB scene file becomes ~1,500 chunks (packets), each with a header: FROM address, TO address, sequence number, checksum. They may take DIFFERENT ROUTES; the receiving machine reassembles by sequence number. If a packet dies, only it is resent. This is why "the internet routes around damage" — a design with no single point of failure:

your laptop → campus router → ISP → [unknown path] → github.com
                 packet 1 ─────────────────→ arrives
                 packet 2 ─────→ lost → resent, different path → arrives
                 packet 3 ────────────────────────→ arrives

TCP vs UDP — the reliability trade.

TCPUDP
GuaranteeAll packets, in order, or noneBest effort; drops are fine
Speed costHandshake, receipts, resendsFire and forget
Used forgit push, web pages, emailGame packets, video calls, voice
Your worldYour repo arrives intact, alwaysA shooter's bullet 10 ms late is DROPPED, never awaited

That game-vs-git split is the exam's favorite tradeoff: a game would rather LOSE a packet than WAIT for one.

DNS — the phone book. github.com is a name for humans; machines route to IP addresses (like 140.82.112.3). DNS is the lookup system that converts, hierarchically, with caching at every level. Trace it yourself:

Socratic

Your git push KNOWS github.com but sends to an IP. Walk the lookup: your machine → its cache → the campus DNS → the root hierarchy → answer cached again. Where is the latency (why is the FIRST push slower than the second), and why do systems cache aggressively?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — see the route. In Terminal:

ping github.com        # DNS happens HERE: name → IP, shown back to you
traceroute github.com  # every router your packets cross (mac: traceroute)

Count the hops; identify your ISP's boundary (where milliseconds jump). Each line is a ROUTER making a local decision with no map of the whole path — the "distributed" in the exam's phrasing.

Step 2 — feel the DNS cache. Ping a site twice. First is slower (lookup); second is cached. Now sudo dscacheutil -flushcache (or your OS's equivalent) and ping again. You just watched cache invalidation — the reason "have you tried turning it off and on" is real engineering.

Step 3 — packets, sized right. The exam loves "why ~1,500 bytes?" (the MTU — the largest frame most links carry; bigger risks fragmentation everywhere, smaller wastes header overhead per byte). Your 2 MB project at 1,500 bytes ≈ 1,400 packets for a push — count them with paper arithmetic. Every push you have made was this exact operation.

Bug Hunt: Network failure modes

  1. git push hangs at "resolving deltas." Deltas = the packets that changed. Why does a push of ONE changed file still involve the WHOLE project's history (what is the pack file — and which organ's job, network or disk, does the waiting happen on)?
  2. You type gihub.com. What did DNS do — and what did your browser do instead (search guess)? Where should the typo have failed, and why did it not?
  3. On school wifi your push is fine; at home it times out. Which TWO layers do you check first (DNS? router? ISP? the site?) — justify the order with traceroute evidence.
  4. The exam classic: "Why is UDP appropriate for a multiplayer game but TCP appropriate for downloading the game?" Answer with the drop-vs-wait trade in one sentence each.
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Design for the network

  1. Design a 2-player co-op turret-defense for the jam era: which messages are UDP-worthy (position updates — old ones are worthless) and which are TCP-worthy (match results)? Label five messages.
  2. What is the LAG-TOLERANT alternative to waiting for the server? (Client-side prediction: your player moves NOW, server corrects later — why does this make your game FEEL 0-lag even at 80 ms?)
  3. Hard: your game's leaderboard (someday) posts a score of 999999. What must the SERVER do — and why is "the client can lie" the single sentence of network security (9.9 bridges here)?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain packets, headers, sequence numbers, and reassembly
  • Choose TCP vs UDP for a given application with reasons
  • Trace DNS resolution and demonstrate the cache
  • Read a traceroute and locate a slowdown's layer
